=== README (60) ===
<!-- markdownlint-disable MD013 -->
# seakarr

Automated Soulseek music downloader with library quality upgrading.

## Features

- **Library quality scanner** — walks your music library directories, reads audio tags (FLAC, MP3, AAC,
  OGG, Opus, WAV, WMA, and more via [lofty](https://crates.io/crates/lofty)), and identifies albums
  whose tracks are in a format outside `filters.allowed_extensions` or fall below the
  configurable bitrate threshold.
- **Upgrade mode** — for each album needing an upgrade, searches the Soulseek network, ranks
  candidates by advertised speed (adjusted by measured-throughput reputation), free-slot bonus, bitrate bonus,
  album-name match and peer reliability, and downloads the best match. The result is written into your
  library when the artist already has a folder under a configured `library.paths` entry, and stays in
  `storage.staging_dir` when it does not; an album selected by `library_upgrade.enabled` is replaced in
  place. An upgrade whose every destination already holds a strictly better file
  keeps those files and still completes the album, so the staging copy is removed without a new file being
  written. A candidate whose files omit the bitrate attribute scores zero on the bitrate bonus once
  `filters.min_bit_rate` is set, so a peer that reports one is preferred; it is still admitted, because its
  real quality is verified after download.
- **Discover mode** — derives the artist list from your library (tags first,
  folder names as the fallback), keeps only the artists that own a folder of
  their own, asks MusicBrainz which conceptual albums each of those is missing,
  and downloads only those. An artist the library only knows as a guest inside
  another artist's folder is skipped, and the run summary reports how many were
  skipped that way; name one explicitly with `--artist` to process it anyway.
  Naming an artist explicitly does not require the library to hold an album for
  it: when a folder named after the artist exists, the artist is processed and
  its albums are placed into that folder, and when there is neither an album nor
  a folder the run warns and keeps the downloads in staging.
  Albums already present are never
  searched or re-downloaded, and each run stops after
  `discover.max_cycle_downloads` download attempts so a large library fills in
  over successive runs. Release types come from `discography.allowed_types`.
- **Manual & batch modes** — search for a specific artist/album on demand, or process a newline-separated
  text file of `artist - album` lines to download a curated wantlist.
  A run places each completed album into the artist's existing library folder when one exists
  anywhere under a configured `library.paths` entry; when the artist has no folder there, or the
  album's destination folder already exists, a manual run keeps the download in
  `storage.staging_dir` (batch and upgrade runs merge into the existing folder instead, keeping
  any file that already parses as audio). An
  album-only request names no artist, so it always stays in staging and says nothing: only manual
  mode can express one, because upgrade mode rejects `--album` on its own and a batch line is trimmed
  before it is parsed, so a line written as `" - Album"` is read as an artist-only line. An artist-naming run with a configured library path explains a
  staging-only download once it has one.
- **Authoritative artist discography** — artist-only manual runs resolve conceptual albums from MusicBrainz
  release groups (cached locally for 30 days) and then run one sequential `Artist Album` Soulseek search per
  eligible album, oldest first. The same authoritative resolution powers `discover` mode for every artist
  it sweeps — those that own a folder named after them. Release categories and optional MusicBrainz artist IDs are configurable; the
  previous folder heuristic remains the explicit opt-out and the visible fallback.
- **Quality filtering** — filter Soulseek results by file extension, minimum
  bitrate, excluded keywords, and upload availability. With
  `download.max_queue_length: 0` a peer must offer a free upload slot; a
  positive limit also admits zero-slot peers until their reported queue
  position can be validated. Path-traversal names are rejected.
- **Peer reputation** — remembers each peer's effective throughput (bytes ÷ transfer time: retry delays plus
  the final transfer, excluding queue wait) and success rate (in SQLite), and ranks search results by a blend
  of advertised and measured throughput plus a reliability factor, so fast, reliable peers are preferred and
  slow or error-prone peers are demoted — regardless of what you search for. Controlled by

# Nested staging album layout

## Problem

A staged album is one directory named `<artist>--<album>` directly under
`storage.staging_dir`, so a download that stays in staging reads as
`downloads/staging/Artist Name--Album Name/01 - Track.flac`. The operator wants the
two components to be real directories instead:
`downloads/staging/Artist Name/Album Name/01 - Track.flac`.

The flattened name is not only cosmetic. It is a lossy encoding of two values into one
path component, and the code that consumes it has to decode it again:

| Site | Behaviour today |
| --- | --- |
| `src/runner.rs:508-516` | Builds `format!("{}--{}", artist.replace(['/','\\'], "-"), album.unwrap_or("unknown").replace(['/','\\'], "-"))` and joins it to the staging root. |
| `src/organizer.rs:516-533` `disc_subdir` | Walks a staged file's parent directories and stops when a directory name `.contains("--")`, because that names the album staging root. An album whose own name contains `--` cannot be told from a boundary by this test. |
| `src/organizer.rs:758-763` `parse_album_slug` | Splits on the first `--` to recover `(artist, album)`; a name without a separator becomes album `"Unknown"`. |
| `src/organizer.rs:774-810` `recover_interrupted_upgrades` | Reads the top level of the staging root, treats every directory as an album slug, re-verifies a `success` album by copying it back, and deletes every other leftover. |
| `src/runner.rs:355-389` `discard_refused_staging` | Removes a refused album's staged files, then prunes directories that are now empty. Its warnings explain the `A--B` + `C` versus `A` + `B--C` slug collapse. |
| `src/runner.rs:392-413` `finish_library_write` | Removes the album staging directory after the album has been written to the library. |

# Nested staging album layout Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use sub-agents (recommended) to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** Stage every download under `<storage.staging_dir>/<artist>/<album>/` instead of `<storage.staging_dir>/<artist>--<album>/`, migrating existing legacy directories on startup.

**Architecture:** A new `src/staging.rs` owns the layout rule (`artist_dir`, `album_dir`), the startup migration (`normalise_layout`, `prepare`) and the staging scan (`scan`, which resolves a sanitised directory name back to the raw `processed_albums` row). `organizer.rs` keeps the sanitiser and the library half of recovery; `runner.rs` and `main.rs` call `staging::prepare` from each mode entry point and derive every album staging path from `staging::album_dir`.

**Tech Stack:** Rust 2024, `rusqlite` (SQLite), `tokio`, `tracing`, `tempfile` for tests. No new dependency.

**Spec:** `docs/agent/specs/2026-10-08-nested-staging-album-layout-design.md` (approved, commit `542309e`).

> **Plan location note:** the invoking chain asked for `docs/plans/`. The repository convention (`AGENTS.md` rule 7, and every plan since `docs/agent/plans/2026-09-09-queue-aware-download-timeouts.md`) is `docs/agent/plans/`. This plan follows the repository convention; `docs/plans/` is a legacy directory holding pre-convention plans only.

---

## Scope Check

Single subsystem. The spec changes the staging path layout in one crate, with one new module. It is not separable into independent plans: the construction site, the decode sites, the migration and the recovery lookup must land together or staging holds two layouts at once and recovery deletes real albums as debris. **No split.**

## File Structure

| File | Responsibility after this change |
| --- | --- |
| `src/staging.rs` (new) | The staging layout rule, the legacy migration, and the staging scan with identity resolution. |
| `src/lib.rs` (modify) | Declare `pub mod staging;`. |
| `src/organizer.rs` (modify) | Keeps `sanitize_component`, `parse_album_slug` (legacy parser), `resume_library_upgrade`. `disc_subdir` gains an album-component parameter; `recover_interrupted_upgrades` iterates `staging::scan`. |
| `src/runner.rs` (modify) | `process_album_internal` builds the nested album path; `finish_library_write` and `discard_refused_staging` prune the artist level; three mode entry points call `staging::prepare`. |
| `src/main.rs` (modify) | `run_batch_mode` calls `staging::prepare`. |
| `src/download.rs` (modify) | One added test assertion only. Production code unchanged. |
| `tests/pipeline_test.rs` (modify) | The end-to-end staging fixture expects the nested tree. |

Order matters: Tasks 1-5 build `staging.rs` with no production caller, so the suite stays green. Task 6 changes `disc_subdir` (its one caller is updated in the same task). Task 7 switches recovery over. Task 8 switches the runner and sweeps the runner test fixtures. Task 9 wires the mode entry points. Task 10 finishes the end-to-end and documentation work.

folder-derived album discovery.

This is the single deliberate divergence from artist-only manual mode, which
falls back to the legacy heuristic. At library scale that fallback would issue
one broad Soulseek search per unresolved artist and could download albums
identified only by peer folder names, which is the misidentification risk the
authoritative design exists to remove. `discography.artist_mbids` remains the
supported fix for a persistently unresolved artist.

### Provider errors skip rather than fall back

A provider error (transport failure, HTTP status, oversized or malformed
response, incomplete pagination, or unusable candidate data) is reported as a
skipped artist for that run. Cached discographies are unaffected, so an outage
only costs the artists that need a network refresh.

If three consecutive artists fail a provider request, the run aborts with an
error instead of grinding through the remainder of the library against a dead
API. An artist served from a *stale* cache counts as a failure whenever the
refresh failed for a provider reason, because the provider was unreachable
behind it; without that rule a warm 30-day cache would hide an outage and the
run would walk the whole library issuing one failing request per artist. A
refresh that failed because the artist no longer resolves is not an outage: it
resets the count, and the cached work list is still used.

A wrong page is treated as a provider defect rather than an unresolvable artist
for the same reason. The one deliberate exception is a search response whose
reported total exceeds the candidates returned: the exact-name match cannot be
proven from the candidates in hand, so that case stays a resolution failure.

### Deterministic artist ordering and spelling
--- 530-560 ---

- **Artist unresolved by MusicBrainz** - skip and report; no broad Soulseek
  search and no legacy fallback. *(Superseded on 2026-10-07 for an explicitly
  named discover artist: the run stops before the library walk with a `Config`
  error naming the artist, because there is no work list to build. The automatic
  sweep still skips and reports, as above.)*
- **Provider error, cached discography available** - use the stale cache and
  warn, as today. *(Superseded on 2026-10-07 for an explicitly named discover
  artist: the same rule applies, and because the verification happens before the
  library walk the cached albums are what the walk is filtered by.)*
- **Provider error, no cache** - skip and report the artist. *(Superseded on
  2026-10-07 for an explicitly named discover artist: the run warns, prints the
  summary and ends before the library walk, with no artist processed.)*
- **Three consecutive provider errors** - abort the run with the failure.
  *(Superseded on 2026-10-07: the abort message also names the artist that
  tripped the breaker.)*
- **Artist resolved, no eligible albums** - not an error; counted.
- **Album present in the library** - not an error; counted and skipped without
  searching.
- **Album with no admissible candidates** - reported as failed; budget not
  charged and the run continues.
- **`discography.enabled: false`** - configuration error at mode resolution.
- **Empty `library.paths`** - configuration error at mode resolution.
- **`--artist` not found in the library** - *(superseded 2026-10-05)* no longer
  a configuration error: a folder named after the artist becomes the
  destination, and with neither an album nor a folder the downloads stay in
  staging with a warning.
- **Blank `--artist`** - configuration error naming the artist.
- **`--album` or `--batch-file` with discover** - configuration error with a
  discover-specific message.
- **Cancellation (SIGINT)** - existing behaviour: stop before the next album and
--- 665-710 ---
### Runner tests (existing `MockClient` and mock provider)

- An album present in the library causes no search and no download.
- A present album does not consume the budget.
- The budget stops the run after N attempts, and artists after the stopping
  point are never examined.
- An album with no admissible candidates does not consume budget and does not
  prevent later albums in the same artist from being attempted.
- An unresolved artist produces no broad artist search and no download.
- A provider error produces a skip, not a legacy fallback.
- Three consecutive provider errors abort the run.
- Selection: an artist that owns no folder of its own is gated out of the
  sweep, the folder's owner is still selected, an artist with one matching
  folder among several is selected, an excluded artist is reported as excluded
  rather than gated, and an explicitly named artist bypasses the gate.
- A successful download emits the usual notification.
- Artist-only manual skips present albums and reports the aggregate notice.
- Artist-only manual with every album present issues no search at all.
- Ordering: artists in normalised-key order, albums oldest first.

### Regression

- All existing auto-mode, manual-mode, batch-mode, scheduled-mode, and
  artist-only discovery tests continue to pass unchanged, except where the
  artist-only presence skip is the intended new behaviour.

## Acceptance criteria

1. `--mode discover` and `search.default_mode: discover` both run gap filling;
   auto mode's behaviour and existing auto-mode tests are untouched.
2. Artists are derived from library tags with folder fallback, aggregator
   exclusions are applied, and the work order is deterministic.
3. Albums already present under a matching folder are never searched or
   downloaded, in both discover and artist-only manual modes.
4. Release types are honoured exactly from `discography.allowed_types`, with no
   new release-type configuration.
5. At most `discover.max_cycle_downloads` download attempts start per run,
   `0` means unlimited, and neither skipped work nor an album with no admissible
   candidates charges the budget.
6. Unresolved or provider-failed artists are reported and never broad-searched;
   three consecutive provider errors abort the run.
7. Per-album notifications are unchanged, and the run summary carries the
   aggregate accounting, including the artist at which the budget stopped.
8. README documents the mode, both configuration keys, the `--artist` filter,
   and the single-instance limitation on scheduling auto and discover together.

Prerequisites preserved: `Harness status: loaded.` and `Project context status: loaded.` are already emitted in this conversation.

## Phase 1 — Root Cause Investigation

### 1. The error message, read literally

```
seakarr: musicbrainz error: Amon Tobin: 3 consecutive MusicBrainz failures; aborting discover run
```

Two producers, both in `src/runner.rs`:

- `abort_discover_run` (`runner.rs:2376-2387`) prints the run summary, then returns `SeakarrError::MusicBrainz("{artist}: 3 consecutive MusicBrainz failures; aborting discover run")`.
- `DISCOVER_PROVIDER_FAILURE_LIMIT: u32 = 3` (`runner.rs:2389`).

`main`'s `exit_code_after_run` (`src/main.rs:159-167`) prints `seakarr: {error}` to **stderr** and exits **code 1**. That is exactly what the operator saw: a summary, then a one-line error, then the shell prompt. There is **no panic, no signal, no abort** of the process image — it is an ordinary `Err` return.

### 2. Reproduction / timeline from the log

The breaker counts *consecutive artists* whose MusicBrainz refresh failed for a provider reason. In this run the three counted events are spread across 5.4 minutes, at the end of the artist sweep:

| Time | Artist | Log line | Counter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 14:34:39 | Afterlife | `discography cache is 38 day(s) old and refresh failed (MusicBrainz returned HTTP 503); using stale cache` | 1 |
| 14:39:57 | Ali B | `MusicBrainz unavailable (MusicBrainz returned HTTP 503); artist skipped` | 2 |
| 14:40:01 | Amon Tobin | `discography cache is 38 day(s) old and refresh failed (MusicBrainz returned HTTP 503); using stale cache` | **3 → abort** |

Reproducible condition: three successive artists whose *refresh* request fails on the provider, with no successful lookup in between. Triggers on any MusicBrainz outage of a few minutes, not just a total outage — the 5-minute gap is Afterlife's download queue timeout (`max_queue_time_secs=300`), not a provider recovery.

### 3. Recent changes

`git log -S DISCOVER_PROVIDER_FAILURE_LIMIT` shows the breaker was introduced by `dc3a9b5 feat: add MusicBrainz library gap filling (discover mode)` and last touched by `93544a0 feat: verify a named discover artist before scanning the library`. It is **not** new: HEAD `4bc7e0e` (v0.33.0) equals `origin/main`, the tree is clean, and this is a long-standing designed path — the nested-staging work (the last release) does not touch it.

### 4. External dependency, with evidence

The log itself records `MusicBrainz returned HTTP 503` four times (`Afterlife`, `Ali B`, `Amon Tobin`, and a failed cache refresh warning earlier). The client is not self-inflicting it: `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs` paces requests **one per second process-wide** (`pace()`, lines 206-217), sets a 10 s timeout, sends a recognised `seakarr/<version>` User-Agent, and retries 5xx **twice** (1 s then 2 s backoff) before classifying a provider failure (`request_json`, lines 242-285). So each counted failure represents three failed attempts over ~10-40 s. Why MusicBrainz returned 503 during that window cannot be recovered after the fact; only that it did is evidenced.

### 5. Data flow trace (where the exit comes from)

`run_discover_mode_with_provider` loop → `discover_artist_albums(...)` → refresh error → `stale_or_legacy` (`discography/mod.rs:1154`) returns `DiscoveryProvenance::StaleCache { age_days, refresh_error, kind: DiscoveryFailure::Provider }` (`mod.rs:613-624`) → `note_stale_cache` (`runner.rs:2543-2574`) **increments** the consecutive counter when `kind == Provider` and returns `true` at 3 → `abort_discover_run` at `runner.rs:2908` (and `2941` for the authoritative-empty branch) → summary printed by `finish_discover_run` → error propagates → `exit_code_after_run` → stderr + exit 1.

### 6. What is actually broken, and what is working as designed

**Working as designed** (and documented): the abort itself. `docs/agent/specs/2026-09-15-musicbrainz-library-gap-filling-design.md:245-258` states the rule explicitly — *"If three consecutive artists fail a provider request, the run aborts… An artist served from a stale cache counts as a failure whenever the refresh failed for a provider reason, because the provider was unreachable behind it; without that rule a warm 30-day cache would hide an outage."* The 2026-09-17 failure-cache spec repeats the counter contract.

**Defect 1 — the summary cannot explain the abort (reporting/accounting).** The two stale-cache failures are counted by the breaker but **never recorded in `counters.provider_failed`**. Only `note_provider_failure` (`runner.rs:2576-2588`) pushes to that vector; `note_stale_cache` (`runner.rs:2543`) increments and warns only. `discover_notices` prints one line per `provider_failed` entry (`src/discover.rs:828-832`). Result: the error claims *3 consecutive failures* and names *Amon Tobin*, while the run summary lists **only Ali B** as provider-failed. The operator's two stale-cache 503s appear solely as WARN lines with no statement that they counted. This is the direct cause of "unclear as to the issue".

**Defect 2 — the summary reads like a completed run.** Nothing marks the run as truncated. `artists_examined` / `artists_total` are printed only when the *download budget* stopped the run (`discover.rs:833-838`); the abort path prints no such notice. At 14:40:01 the sweep was still at "A…" alphabetically (1338 albums, 18 134 files scanned; 60 artists gated out, 29 albums present), so the summary's counts describe a small prefix of the library while looking final.

**Behavioural asymmetry worth recording (not necessarily a defect).** Failure #1 (Afterlife) was accepted and its stale work list *used* — the log shows `Processing: Afterlife — Afterlife` and a real download attempt. Failure #3 (Amon Tobin) aborted **before** `fill_artist_gap`, discarding the very stale list that had just been judged usable. The same event is therefore incremental at count 1-2 and destructive at count 3.

### 7. Explicitly ruled out as causes

- **Not a panic/crash**: no `panicked at`, no `SIGSEGV`/`SIGABRT`, no `thread 'main'` message.
- **Not the peer connection reset** (`djdownloadme`, `os error 104`) or **`[listener] failed to get peer address`**: per-peer network noise; the client logged `Disconnecting` and continued.
- **Not the download queue timeout**: recorded as one failed album (`Afterlife — Afterlife (all candidates exhausted: … max_queue_time_secs=300)`), a per-album outcome that never aborts a run.
- **Not `--ignore-processed`**: `Ignoring already-processed record: Afterlife — Afterlife` followed by `Processing` is that flag's normal behaviour (the processed row is ignored so the album is retried).
- **Not the nested-staging release (v0.33.0)**: no staging/recovery code is on this path.
- **Not self-inflicted rate limiting**: see §4 (1 req/s pacing, honoured `Retry-After` on 429, only 5xx reaches this path).

### 8. Root-cause statement

The discover run exited **by design**: MusicBrainz returned 503 on the refresh of three consecutive artists' discographies (Afterlife, Ali B, Amon Tobin), the documented `DISCOVER_PROVIDER_FAILURE_LIMIT = 3` circuit breaker tripped, and the run returned `SeakarrError::MusicBrainz` → exit code 1. What is genuinely broken is the **accounting around the abort**, not the abort: stale-cache provider failures increment the breaker without entering the counters that the summary reports, and no notice marks the run as truncated — so the final message contradicts the summary it printed two lines earlier.

## Decision needed

The fix scope is a real choice: the abort semantics are documented spec, while the reporting gap is a defect in it.

## Introduction

MusicBrainz has finite resources and wishes to make the MusicBrainz database available to as much of the Internet community as possible. However, at certain times of day the number of requests to the [MusicBrainz API](/doc/MusicBrainz_API) exceeds our capacity for handling these requests. Honoring all of these requests would overload our servers and degrade the service for everyone. For this reason we rate limit our Web Service, which limits the number of requests that clients can make in a given period of time.

## How throttling works

We may change the blocking/throttling rules at any time in order to protect the overall site health.

As of 2012-01-08 our rules are as follows:

When a request reaches our servers we check three conditions, in the following order:

1.  User-Agent string: are we receiving too many requests from this application?
2.  Source IP address: are we receiving too many requests from this particular IP address?
3.  Global: are the MusicBrainz servers as a whole too busy to handle this request?

If the answer to any one of those questions is "yes", then the request is denied with a 503 Service Unavailable error, and processing stops. Otherwise, we continue to the next check. If all checks pass then the request is honoured.

Read on for details of how each check works.

### User-Agent

For user-agents associated with [headphones](https://github.com/rembo10/headphones/wiki): we allow through (on average) 50 requests per second, and decline (http 503) the rest. This includes headphones itself, across several versions, as well as beets, the tagger it uses, when we can determine it's been called by headphones.

For "python-musicbrainz/0.7.3": we allow through (on average) 50 requests per second, and decline the rest (though recently this has not been hit).

For "anonymous" user-agents (see below): we allow through (on average) 50 requests per second, and decline (http 503) the rest.

For other user-agents: allow through.

### Source IP address

Unless you have agreed otherwise with MusicBrainz, the rule is as follows:

The rate at which your IP address is making requests is measured. If that rate is too high, **all** your requests will be declined (http 503) until the rate drops again. Currently that rate is (on average) 1 request per second.

For example: if your requests are coming in at 4 requests per second, we don't honour 25% of them and decline the other 75% - we decline 100% of them, until the rate drops to 1 per second or lower.

### Global

We allow through 300 requests each second (on average), and decline (http 503) the rest.

## More about User-Agent throttling

Applications which misbehave can end up degrading the quality of the MusicBrainz service; such applications (based on their User-Agent header) may be subject to throttling specific to that application.

If we see an application that's misbehaving, we like to try to get in touch with its maintainers to address the problem. Therefore, _there needs to be enough information in the User-Agent string for us to contact the maintainers_.

User-Agents which break this rule are what we call "anonymous". The anonymous User-Agents, and therefore the ones subject to the throttling described earlier, are:

User-Agent String

Version

<blank>

\-

Java

any

Python-urllib

any

Jakarta Commons-HttpClient

any

Apache-HttpClient

UNAVAILABLE (java 1.4)

## How can I be a good citizen and be smart about using the Web Service?

("How do I avoid getting blocked?" / "I'm blocked! How do I get un-blocked?").

To avoid being blocked or throttled by MusicBrainz, applications should follow the advice below. If you're using an application maintained by someone else, you may need to contact the maintainers to get them to fix any problems.

If you are an application author and your application has been blocked or throttled, and none of the information on this page helped you resolve the problem, please [contact us](/doc/ContactUs) to talk about the problem.

### Provide meaningful User-Agent strings

_Each request sent to MusicBrainz needs to include a User-Agent header, with enough information in the User-Agent for us (MusicBrainz) to contact the application maintainers._ We strongly suggest including your application's version number in the User-Agent string too.

This is so that if there's a problem we can contact you. We suggest that your User-Agent string should look like:

Application name/<version> ( contact-url )

or

Application name/<version> ( contact-email )

Two examples:

MyAwesomeTagger/1.2.0 ( [http://myawesometagger.example.com](http://myawesometagger.example.com) )
MyAwesomeTagger/1.2.0 ( me@example.com )

Our client libraries now support functions for setting the User-Agent string. If you are using one of [our libraries](/doc/Developer_Resources), you will need to add a call to set the User-Agent string via the library and your application should work again.

### Scheduling

Please refrain from having your applications wake up at a certain time of the day to perform some action. For instance, having your application wake up at 03:00 local time and query a lot of data at MusicBrainz is _a bad idea_. If this application gets distributed to many users around the globe (e.g. in a Linux distribution), then at various times around the clock, but always at the beginning of the hour, MusicBrainz will be overloaded with requests from your application. Also, 03:00 in your timezone might be the peak time for MusicBrainz somewhere else in the world. If you program your application this way and it impacts our service, we will block your application.

If there is a task you would like to perform in the background and are tempted to do it at an off-peak time, you should have your application make calls at random intervals throughout the day. If the application spreads its calls throughout the day, it spreads the load on the MusicBrainz servers across the day as well and avoids creating artificial peak times.

### Checking for changes

If you want your application to poll MusicBrainz to see if some metadata has changed, _please don't do this_. > [@PoQStacker](#): > > What does the X-RateLimit-Reset value mean? That’s the time before the rate limit is reset (in UTC epoch seconds). T+0 we start to count incoming requests T+2 we reset that count If the number of requests reach the limit between T+0 and T+2 subsequent requests are refused, until we reach T+2, then we start again to count (and allow), rinse and repeat. That’s for the global limit, at the moment we have enough resources and this limit shouldn’t be an issue. We enforce limits per IP & User Agent too, if the recommended rate is respected, a fair user shouldn’t hit this limit either. A proper user agent string allowing the application owner to be contacted is required. But, in any case, it is heavily recommended to properly handle error codes in your application, as limits may be hit due to high traffic, or because we lowered them temporarily (for example if we have issues with backend load). In case of 503, pause and retry. One may also use those X-RateLimit-\* headers to make it smarter. Unfair use is not recommended (at all). ---

Prerequisites preserved (`Harness status: loaded.`, `Project context status: loaded.`). Phase 1 continues — the 503 itself, with live evidence.

## Why MusicBrainz returned 503 — findings

### 1. A 503 from MusicBrainz is not "the site is down"

MusicBrainz's own rate-limiting documentation (fetched live: `musicbrainz.org/doc/MusicBrainz_API/Rate_Limiting`) states that a request is denied with **503 Service Unavailable** when *any* of three checks fail, in this order:

1. **User-Agent** — too many requests from this application (only `headphones`, `python-musicbrainz/0.7.3` and anonymous UAs are on that list; *"For other user-agents: allow through"*).
2. **Source IP** — *"Currently that rate is (on average) 1 request per second… we decline 100% of them, until the rate drops"*.
3. **Global** — *"We allow through 300 requests each second (on average), and decline (http 503) the rest."*

So a 503 can mean "your IP was too fast", "your app is throttled", **or** "MusicBrainz as a whole is too busy". seakarr currently cannot tell which — see §4.

### 2. MusicBrainz's search cluster is documented as overloaded right now

From MetaBrainz staff on the official status thread (fetched live, `community.metabrainz.org/t/musicbrainz-current-status/815551`):

- *"Our search servers are aging and overloaded… you will indeed see more 503 errors on API searches than usual"* (reosarevok, 2026-09-11).
- *"sometimes global rate limiter is triggering because of sudden high number of queries. We had to hard cap more than usual to protect our search servers, and we're working on setting up a new cluster (but it will not be operational before end of November this year)"* (Zas, 2026-09-11).
- Other app authors report the same: Mp3tag *"often (maybe even most of the time) I see HTTP 503 or timeouts"*; a second developer *"I have to retry this ~3 times every time"* (Sept 2026).

seakarr uses exactly that path: `search_artists` requests `/ws/2/artist?query=artist:"…"` (`src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:288+`), which is the query endpoint the thread names. The reported run is 2026-10-26, i.e. **inside** that known degradation window.

### 3. seakarr's own request volume cannot have caused a per-IP limit

From the code:

- One process-wide 1 req/s gate: `REQUEST_INTERVAL = Duration::from_secs(1)` (`musicbrainz.rs:10`) plus a process-wide `OnceLock` gate (`production_request_gate`, `musicbrainz.rs:158-161`), so even several provider instances in one process share one slot per second.
- Requests are sequential (`request_json` awaited per call; no concurrency).
- User-Agent is compliant: `seakarr/0.33.0 (https://github.com/binhex/seakarr)` (`musicbrainz.rs:189-192`) — matches the documented `Name/version ( contact-url )` form, and is not on MB's throttled list.

From the log: the sweep examined 10 artists between 14:32:04 and 14:40:01 (477 s), issuing roughly 15-20 HTTP requests (one search per artist, plus release-groups for resolved ones, plus 3 attempts per failed request). That is **~0.03-0.04 req/s average, peak 1 req/s** — two orders of magnitude below the 1 req/s sustained limit that triggers a per-IP block. **seakarr alone did not rate-limit itself into 503s.**

### 4. The provider was healthy 50 seconds earlier and healthy again afterwards

- Live verdicts landed right before the failures: `30Hz` (14:32:04), `A Break From The Norm` (14:32:07), `A Forest Mighty Black` (14:32:07), `A. Skillz` (14:33:48), `A.Skillz And Krafty Kuts` (14:33:49) — all "could not be resolved", which requires a **live** MusicBrainz answer (cached failures are logged differently). First 503: 14:34:39, ~50 s later.
- I probed the same endpoint live: `GET /ws/2/artist?query=artist:"Amon Tobin"` → **HTTP 200**, 2 candidates, `date: Mon, 26 Oct 2026 15:26:27 GMT`, response headers `x-ratelimit-limit: 400`, `x-ratelimit-remaining: 374`, `x-ratelimit-reset: 1793028384`, `x-mb-gateway: rex`, `x-cache-status: MISS`. Time to first byte: 3.9 s (slow, but serving).

So the condition was **transient** (first failure 14:34:39, recovered well before 15:26) and **provider-side**, not a permanent block of the seakarr UA.

### 5. What seakarr does wrong *in response* to a 503 (this part is ours)

This does not cause the 503, but it converts a short overload window into a dead run, and it destroys the evidence needed to answer "is it global or are we blocked?":

1. **Retries inside the block window.** `request_json` (`musicbrainz.rs:242-285`) retries a 5xx after 1 s then 2 s, then gives up. MetaBrainz's own guidance (dev forum, fetched live): *"Retrying your request before X-RateLimit-Reset time is very likely to fail"* and *"In case of 503, pause and retry. One may also use those X-RateLimit-* headers to make it smarter."* A rate-limit window is ~2 s (or longer), so all three attempts typically land inside it and the artist is scored as an "outage".
2. **`Retry-After` is honoured only for 429, never for 503.** `parse_retry_after` is called solely in the `status.as_u16() == 429` branch (`musicbrainz.rs:260-268`); the 5xx branch ignores it. If MB sends `Retry-After` on a rate-limit 503, seakarr discards it.
3. **The 503's body and rate-limit headers are thrown away.** `DiscographyError::HttpStatus(u16)` (`discography/mod.rs:109-110`) carries only the status code; the response body and headers are dropped. MetaBrainz documents that a 503 carries `X-RateLimit-Zone: global` (= servers overloaded) or `per-ip` (= this IP is too fast) — the single piece of information that would settle "is it a site error or are we being blocked?" is exactly what seakarr does not keep.
4. **The breaker then fires on that.** `note_stale_cache` (`runner.rs:2543-2574`) and `note_provider_failure` (`runner.rs:2576-2588`) count each such artist, and at 3 the run aborts. With MB's search cluster hard-capped until ~end of November 2026, three artists in a row hitting the overload window is likely, not exceptional.

### 6. What remains genuinely undetermined (and can be settled)

The log cannot distinguish **global overload** from **per-IP denial**, because that distinction lives in the 503's `X-RateLimit-Zone` header, which seakarr discards. seakarr's own volume rules out self-inflicted limiting from *this process*; it does not rule out the host's **public IP being shared** — a VPN egress, or another MusicBrainz client on the same machine (beets, Picard, Lidarr, a scheduled seakarr cycle). MetaBrainz staff diagnose such cases by IP (*"It's more like your IP is blocked… email to support with your IP"*). If the Tower shares its IP with other MB clients, a per-IP block is plausible; if not, this was the documented search-cluster overload.

### 7. Root-cause statement (revised)

The 503s were **MusicBrainz-side**: its search cluster is documented as overloaded and hard-capped through November 2026, and the run's own request rate (~0.03 req/s) rules seakarr out as the cause. What seakarr owns is the **handling**: it retries inside the rate-limit window instead of honouring `Retry-After`/`X-RateLimit-Reset`, discards the `X-RateLimit-Zone`/body that would identify a per-IP block, and lets a transient overload trip a run-aborting breaker — while the summary cannot explain which events counted. That handling gap is what made a short provider hiccup cost a 17-minute run with no diagnosable trace.

Two decisions follow.

## Phase 1 complete — root cause confirmed

Your answers close the last open branch: **no VPN, no other MusicBrainz clients on that IP**. seakarr had the egress IP to itself, and its own traffic was ~0.03 req/s against a 1 req/s allowance. That eliminates the per-IP explanation from the operator's side, so the remaining explanation is the one MusicBrainz documents about itself.

### Root cause

**Trigger (external):** MusicBrainz's search cluster is overloaded and hard-capped. MetaBrainz staff state on the official status thread that API *search* requests (`/ws/2/artist?query=…` — the exact call seakarr makes) *"will indeed see more 503 errors than usual"*, that *"we had to hard cap more than usual to protect our search servers"*, and that the replacement cluster *"will not be operational before end of November this year"*. The run (2026-10-26) sits inside that window. The 503 is MB's documented response to a **global** capacity check, not to anything seakarr did.

**Failure path (internal):** 503 → `request_json` retries after 1 s and 2 s, both inside MB's ~2 s rate-limit window → `DiscographyError::HttpStatus(503)` → `stale_or_legacy` classifies it `DiscoveryFailure::Provider` → `note_stale_cache` / `note_provider_failure` increment the breaker → third artist → `abort_discover_run` → exit 1.

**Why it cost the whole run:** MB's own guidance for a 503 is *"pause and retry"* and *"retrying before `X-RateLimit-Reset` is very likely to fail"*. seakarr pauses 1-2 s (not until reset), never reads `Retry-After` or `X-RateLimit-Reset` on a 5xx (only on 429), and discards the `X-RateLimit-Zone` header and body that would say `global` vs `per-ip`. Three artists inside one overload window therefore look like a sustained outage.

**Explicitly excluded as causes:** seakarr's request rate (self-measured from the log), its compliant `seakarr/0.33.0 (https://github.com/binhex/seakarr)` User-Agent, the peer connection reset, the Afterlife queue timeout, `--ignore-processed`, and the v0.33.0 staging change. No panic, no signal — an ordinary `Err` → exit 1.

### Fix scope for the chain (your choice: "Handle 503 per MB guidance")

Not implemented here — this step is investigation only. The fix step should treat these as the targets:

| Target | Required behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:242-285` `request_json` | On 5xx, honour `Retry-After` when present and `X-RateLimit-Reset` when present (currently both are read only in the 429 branch); back off past the stated window with jitter instead of 1 s/2 s fixed. |
| `src/discography/mod.rs:105-125` `DiscographyError` | Carry the diagnostic detail (status, `X-RateLimit-Zone` if present, reset instant, bounded body excerpt) instead of a bare `HttpStatus(u16)`, so the warning names whether MB is globally overloaded or denying this IP. |
| `src/runner.rs:2543-2588` breaker accounting | Only strike the breaker once the retries are genuinely exhausted — i.e. after the honoured wait, not after ~3 s of blind retries. |

### One residual finding stays open (out of this run's scope)

The **summary/accounting defect** identified earlier is *not* covered by the chosen scope: stale-cache provider failures increment the breaker but never enter `counters.provider_failed`, so the abort message *"3 consecutive MusicBrainz failures"* still contradicts a summary that lists only Ali B, and no notice marks the run as truncated. That is a reporting fix, not a 503 fix — flag it for a separate spec/run rather than bundling it here, unless you say otherwise.

Chain hand-off: Phase 1 is done, the root cause is a documented MusicBrainz search-cluster overload amplified by seakarr's 503 handling, and the accepted scope is to handle 503s the way MetaBrainz prescribes. No files were modified and no subagents were dispatched.

Apply the TDD skill exactly as written, including the Iron Law, the
red-green-refactor cycle, and the RED verification steps. Do not substitute a
workflow of your own.

Do NOT skip the RED phase, and do NOT write production code before the failing
test. Report the tests written and their results. This step handles
implementation and testing only; do NOT dispatch subagents for review or
verification.

**If you need a user decision** (e.g. architectural choice before implementing,
which test approach to take): use `ask_user_question` to present it. Do NOT
write the question in prose and expect the chain to wait; the chain will not
stop.

A configured ID takes precedence over name search. If it differs from the cached identity, the cache row is
ignored and refreshed.

**Q: What are the current MusicBrainz discovery limits?**

The integration deliberately favors safe fallback over guessing:

- Artist search reads at most 100 candidates. If MusicBrainz reports more, seakarr cannot prove the exact-name
  match is unique, so it uses compatible stale cache or the clearly warned legacy fallback.
- Configuration validates an MBID's UUID shape, not its existence. A well-formed ID that MusicBrainz does not
  recognize is retried on a later stale/uncached run and follows the normal visible fallback path; failed IDs
  are not negatively cached.
- The SQLite cache keeps one bounded row per normalized artist queried and has no automatic eviction. A later
  refresh replaces that artist's row atomically.
- `Retry-After` accepts integer delay-seconds from 0 through 30. HTTP-date, malformed, or larger values are
  treated as provider unavailability so an external response cannot cause an unbounded wait.

**Q: What happens when MusicBrainz cannot resolve an artist from my library?**

In `discover` mode a swept artist is skipped for that run and reported in the run
summary: no broad Soulseek artist search is issued and no folder-derived
discovery is attempted, so albums are never downloaded from an unverified
identity. An artist named with `--artist` is resolved before the library is walked
instead, so a name MusicBrainz cannot resolve stops the run with a configuration
error naming the artist and no summary. A name MusicBrainz cannot resolve has two
fixes. The first is to name the artist by a code instead: an ISNI such as
`0000 0004 6659 7022`, an IPI such as `00581977202`, or the MusicBrainz artist
ID. An ISNI or IPI is resolved against exactly one MusicBrainz artist that
carries it, and a MusicBrainz ID by exact entity lookup; neither falls back to
the folder heuristic, so neither can fail the way an ambiguous name does. The
precise fix is a pinned `discography.artist_mbids` entry — keyed by the artist

TDD cycle complete. Both prerequisites were already emitted (`Harness status: loaded.`, `Project context status: loaded.`) and are preserved.

## RED — tests written first, watched fail

Added to `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs` tests (plus one existing test retargeted to the new contract):

| Test | Encodes |
| --- | --- |
| `server_error_honors_retry_after` | A 503 carrying `Retry-After: 3` must not be retried before 3 s (local backoff would be 1 s) |
| `server_error_honors_rate_limit_reset` | A 503 carrying `X-RateLimit-Reset` (+4 s epoch) must wait the reset, not 1 s |
| `server_error_prefers_the_longer_rate_limit_hint` | `Retry-After: 1` must not override a later reset — the longer pause wins |
| `server_error_hint_beyond_the_cap_is_not_retried` | `Retry-After: 120` → exactly one attempt, no sleep, error names the wait |
| `server_error_detail_names_the_rate_limit_zone_and_body` | `HTTP 503` must carry `X-RateLimit-Zone: global` and the body text |
| `server_error_body_capture_is_bounded` | A 4 KiB body is excerpted to ≤256 chars (not swallowed, not trusted whole) |
| `exhausted_server_errors_return_last_status` (updated) | An exhausted 503 is now a `ProviderError`, not a bare `HttpStatus` |

**Verified RED** — `cargo test --lib discography::musicbrainz::tests::server_error` → 1 passed, 6 failed, each for the expected reason:

```
the 503 retry must wait the three-second Retry-After, waited 2s
the 503 retry must wait for the rate-limit reset, waited 2s
the reset must outrank a shorter Retry-After, waited 2s
a retry hint past the cap must not be retried inside the window  (left: 3, right: 1)
the 503 must say which rate-limit zone denied it, got MusicBrainz returned HTTP 503
the start of the 503 body must be kept, got MusicBrainz returned HTTP 503
```

## GREEN — minimal implementation

- `src/discography/mod.rs` — new `DiscographyError::ProviderError { status, detail }`; keeps `HttpStatus(u16)` for 429/4xx, so no existing behaviour changes. Its `Display` is the same string as before when the response carries nothing.
- `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs` — `server_retry_hint()` (later of `Retry-After` and `X-RateLimit-Reset`), `provider_error()` (zone + bounded body excerpt + the requested wait), and the 5xx branch now sleeps the server's pause instead of a fixed 1 s/2 s, or returns immediately with the wait when it exceeds the 30 s cap.
- `README.md` — the retry bullet now documents the 5xx hint behaviour too (it previously described 429 only).

**Verified GREEN** — `cargo test --lib discography::musicbrainz::tests::` → 38 passed, 0 failed. Full suite → **1378 tests, 0 failed** across all 9 targets. `cargo fmt --check` clean, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean, `cargo llvm-cov --fail-under-lines 95` → **97.14 %** lines. `markdownlint README.md` exit 0.

## Notes for the chain

- **One test failure was my test's fault, not the code's.** The first "cap" run reported 3 requests; file instrumentation showed reqwest's 10 s timeout firing because a paused-clock runtime auto-advances while idle. The test now spins on the first response before advancing. No production code changed for that.
- **Deliberate deviation from the option text:** no random jitter. The server's own reset is the safe pause, a single client cannot form a herd, and bounded jitter cannot be asserted deterministically without adding a dependency or a nondeterministic test. Exponential 1 s/2 s backoff remains for 5xx responses that name no pause. Say the word if you want jitter anyway.
- **Out of scope, still open:** the summary/accounting gap (stale-cache provider failures increment the breaker but never enter `counters.provider_failed`, and no notice marks an aborted run) was excluded from the agreed fix scope. The new error text now reaches the operator through the existing WARN line and the `provider failed for …` notice, but the summary still lists only non-stale-cache failures.
- Nothing staged, no commits made; the fix step stops here for the chain's verification.

are outside this split-disc check. Success rows created by older versions under
a single-disc album label are ignored by normalized history matching; rerun the
album to replace that partial result.

**Q: Does MusicBrainz require an account or API key?**

No. Seakarr sends an identifying User-Agent and paces requests to at most one per second, following the
[MusicBrainz rate-limiting guidance](https://musicbrainz.org/doc/MusicBrainz_API/Rate_Limiting). Normal reads
need no credential, and no new secret is added to `seakarr.yml`.

**Q: How do I pin an ambiguous artist name to a MusicBrainz ID?**

Add the artist name and its canonical hyphenated UUID to `discography.artist_mbids`. Keys are matched after
the same normalization used for automatic artist matching:

```yaml
discography:
  enabled: true
  cache_days: 30
  allowed_types: [studio_album, live_album]
  artist_mbids:
    "Nirvana": "5b11f4ce-a62d-471e-81fc-a69a8278c7da"
```

A configured ID takes precedence over name search. If it differs from the cached identity, the cache row is
ignored and refreshed.

**Q: What are the current MusicBrainz discovery limits?**

The integration deliberately favors safe fallback over guessing:

- Artist search reads at most 100 candidates. If MusicBrainz reports more, seakarr cannot prove the exact-name
  match is unique, so it uses compatible stale cache or the clearly warned legacy fallback.
- Configuration validates an MBID's UUID shape, not its existence. A well-formed ID that MusicBrainz does not
  recognize is retried on a later stale/uncached run and follows the normal visible fallback path; failed IDs
  are not negatively cached.
- The SQLite cache keeps one bounded row per normalized artist queried and has no automatic eviction. A later
  refresh replaces that artist's row atomically.
- Retries are bounded by the response's own rate-limit headers. A 429 waits its integer `Retry-After`
  (0-30 s); an HTTP-date, malformed, or larger value is treated as provider unavailability so an external
  response cannot cause an unbounded wait. A 5xx waits the pause it names: the later of `Retry-After` and
  `X-RateLimit-Reset`. A pause beyond 30 s is reported instead of sat on, and the warning carries the
  `X-RateLimit-Zone` (a global overload rather than a per-IP limit) and a bounded excerpt of the body.

**Q: What happens when MusicBrainz cannot resolve an artist from my library?**

In `discover` mode a swept artist is skipped for that run and reported in the run
summary: no broad Soulseek artist search is issued and no folder-derived
discovery is attempted, so albums are never downloaded from an unverified
identity. An artist named with `--artist` is resolved before the library is walked
instead, so a name MusicBrainz cannot resolve stops the run with a configuration
error naming the artist and no summary. A name MusicBrainz cannot resolve has two
fixes. The first is to name the artist by a code instead: an ISNI such as
`0000 0004 6659 7022`, an IPI such as `00581977202`, or the MusicBrainz artist
ID. An ISNI or IPI is resolved against exactly one MusicBrainz artist that
carries it, and a MusicBrainz ID by exact entity lookup; neither falls back to
the folder heuristic, so neither can fail the way an ambiguous name does. The
precise fix is a pinned `discography.artist_mbids` entry — keyed by the artist
name, `isni:<digits>`, `ipi:<digits>` or `mbid:<uuid>` and holding the MusicBrainz
UUID —
which also selects a single artist when a shared IPI or ISNI has several
carriers. A code that resolved is logged with the canonical name, the MBID and
any disambiguation comment, so the identity it picked is visible. Three
consecutive MusicBrainz request failures abort
the run instead, so a provider outage cannot grind through the rest of the
library.

### Finding 1 — MEDIUM: the elapsed-reset test cannot fail if the zero-hint filter is removed

`src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:1479-1487` (`server_error_with_an_elapsed_reset_waits_the_backoff`)

The test claims to pin "Zero is not a licence to retry immediately", but its only timing assertion is `advanced >= Duration::from_secs(1)`, and `advance_until` (`:1140-1155`) increments and advances **before** it ever yields:

```rust
let advanced = advance_until(|| success_hits == 1 || task.is_finished(), 8s).await;
assert!(advanced >= Duration::from_secs(1), ...);
```

There is no yield between `spin_until(error_hits == 1)` returning and the first `done()` evaluation, so the first check is always `false`, the loop advances one second, and then 10 000 yields let the retry land. Delete `.filter(|wait| !wait.is_zero())` at `:529` (i.e. reinstate the round‑1 bug) and the test still goes green: `hint = Some(0)` → `sleep(0)` → retry completes inside that first advance window → `advanced == 1s` → assertion satisfied, `success_hits == 1`, `Ok`. Correct behaviour: after the first 503, keep the runtime busy for a bounded window and assert the retry has **not** happened, e.g. before `:1479`:

```rust
for _ in 0..10_000 { tokio::task::yield_now().await; }
assert_eq!(success_hits.load(Ordering::SeqCst), 0,
    "an elapsed reset must not licence an immediate retry");
```

Related, same branch family: the `Retry-After: 0` half of the fix (`:517`) has **no** 5xx test at all — every `"retry-after", "0"` in the module is a 429 (`:1085-1094`), which takes the unrelated `parse_retry_after` path.

`src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:498-533`, README.md:1129-1135

The whole feature rests on "`X-RateLimit-Reset` is the epoch second the window reopens" (`:499`, `:519-528`) and on `X-RateLimit-Zone` existing (`:546`). Nothing in the repo — README, `docs/`, or a doc link near the code — establishes either; the tests (`:1224-1268`, `:1437-1480`) encode the same epoch-seconds assumption as the code, so they cannot detect a wrong unit. The failure modes are asymmetric and both bad: if the header is delta-seconds, `epoch.saturating_sub(now)` is always 0 → filtered → the client silently retries 1 s into a closed window (the exact behaviour this change exists to remove); if it is a millisecond epoch, `hint > 30s` on every hinted 5xx → one attempt, no retry, for every 503. `X-RateLimit-Zone` is harmless if it does not exist, but then the README's promised zone clause is dead.

Smallest fix: name the source in the function doc (the README already links `https://musicbrainz.org/doc/MusicBrainz_API/Rate_Limiting`, README:1098) so the unit is reviewable, and confirm once against that page. I could not verify the header semantics from anything in this checkout.

`src/discography/mod.rs:118-121`

- A body read failure produces `"<body omitted>"` (`musicbrainz.rs:574-575`), which becomes `detail` although it names nothing the response carried — the doc's "otherwise `detail` names what the response carried" is false there.

Smallest fix: reword to "`detail` is empty when the response said nothing usable: no zone, no pause hint, and no printable body text; a body that could not be read is reported as `<body omitted>`".

### Finding 4 — LOW: the rate-limit zone is neither sanitised nor bounded, unlike the body in the same message

`src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:544-550` vs `:551-576`

The body is control-stripped, whitespace-collapsed and cut to 256 chars on the stated grounds that this text "reaches the operator's terminal and log file"; the zone header is only `trim()`-ed and copied verbatim (`:549`), and is unbounded (header values may be several KB). `HeaderValue::to_str()` is the only filter, and it admits HTAB, so an interior tab survives into the single-line message; a large zone yields a huge error string.

Smallest fix: run `zone` through the same collapse (`split_whitespace().join(" ")`) and a length cap before pushing it at `:579`.

### Finding 5 — LOW: the body sanitiser misses Unicode format characters

`src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:558-568` (test comment at `:1576-1579`)

`char::is_control()` is Unicode general category Cc only. Newlines, tabs, NUL, ESC and C1 controls are correctly neutralised, and U+2028/U+2029 are removed by `split_whitespace()`, but category Cf survives: a body containing U+202E (RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE), U+200B–U+200F or U+2066–U+2069 reaches the terminal/log through a message whose comment justifies the stripping with "a hostile proxy can answer a 5xx with an ANSI escape sequence" — a bidi override is the same class of hostile payload and can visually reorder the rest of the log line.

Smallest fix: map those ranges to `' '` as well (e.g. `'\u{200B}'..='\u{200F}' | '\u{202A}'..='\u{202E}' | '\u{2066}'..='\u{2069}'`).

### Finding 6 — LOW: a legitimate HTTP-date `Retry-After` is discarded and never reported

`src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:511-517`, README.md:1132

Falling back to the backoff is the stated requirement, so the wait itself is per spec. What is *not* required is losing the hint entirely: for `Retry-After: Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT` the operator gets `MusicBrainz returned HTTP 503 (… body: …)` with no mention of a pause, so "the operator needs the wait in the message" (`:288-290`) fails for one of the two legal forms. `chrono` is already a dependency, so parsing IMF-fixdate is available; the cheap half-fix is to append a sanitised `retry-after: <raw>` part when the value exists but is unusable.

`src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:1230-1236`, `:1278-1284`, `:1437-1443`

The hint is recomputed against `SystemTime::now()` when the 503 lands (`:523-527`), while the test fixes `reset = wall_now + 6` and asserts `advanced >= 4s`. That leaves only 2 s of real-time slack: a stall of >2 s between `MockServer::start`/header creation and the response being processed (contended CI, parallel test threads, debug build) shrinks the hint below the assertion and fails a correct implementation. Using `+10` and asserting `>= 6s` keeps the same discriminating power (backoff(0)=1 s still fails by 5 s) with 4 s of slack and stays under the 30 s cap. `server_error_prefers_retry_after_when_it_is_later` is immune because `Retry-After: 5` dominates either way.

## Review

Scope: I read `/tmp/review.diff` in full, then the current tree: `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs` (constants 9‑30, `pace`/`read_limited` 222‑260, `request_json` 267‑320, `backoff`/`server_retry_hint` 497‑550, `provider_error` 552‑608, `single_line` 610‑648, `parse_retry_after` 650‑664, and the whole test module 666‑2470), `src/discography/mod.rs` (`DiscographyError` 107‑152, `is_stable_artist_resolution_failure` 652‑677, `DiscoveryFailure::from_error` 679‑695, failure-cache write 1090‑1122, classification test 3612‑3637), `README.md:1120‑1136`, `Cargo.toml` (MSRV 1.88 — `Option::is_none_or` is fine). I also confirmed the working tree matches the supplied diff (`watchdog_diff --stat`: README +10, mod.rs +12, musicbrainz.rs +897). No files were edited.

### Correct (verified, not merely trusted)
- Retry loop arithmetic is sound: `hint` is `Option<Duration>` (Copy), so `is_none_or` + later `hint.unwrap_or_else(...)` cannot double-move; `attempt == 2 || !within_cap` makes the >cap path exactly one request (musicbrainz.rs:298‑305), and `attempt == 2` is still reached only after two sleeps.
- No overflow/underflow: `epoch.saturating_sub(now)`, `Duration::from_secs(u64::MAX)` is valid, comparisons are `Duration`-typed, and the byte slice is `&[u8][..min(..)]`, so a split UTF‑8 sequence yields U+FFFD via `from_utf8_lossy` rather than a panic (musicbrainz.rs:573‑576).
- No unbounded wait: the error body read is inside `reqwest`'s 10 s total timeout, and every `sleep` is ≤30 s; `pace()` releases its mutex before the request.
- Classification unchanged: `from_error`'s wildcard still maps `ProviderError` to `DiscoveryFailure::Provider` (mod.rs:688‑694); `is_stable_artist_resolution_failure` still matches only `ArtistUnresolved`, so a 5xx is never written to the failure cache (mod.rs:674‑676, 1110‑1112). No in-repo caller matches `HttpStatus` for 5xx (grep: only 429/other-4xx sites).
- Round‑2 fix 1 is genuinely guarded: with the `.filter(|w| !w.is_zero())` on the reset removed, the elapsed test's pre-advance `success_hits == 0` check fails (musicbrainz.rs:1536‑1547); the two `Retry-After: 0` / HTTP‑date tests have the same guard.
- Round‑2 fixes 2/6 exist with distinct decision boundaries (cap-inclusive 30 vs over-cap 31, max in both directions, reset-only, elapsed, zero, HTTP‑date, quoted unusable value, exhaustion qualifier, zone collapse+bound, body bound 256 with a tight 256/257 pair).

### Findings

**1. MEDIUM — the two reset tests are coupled to the real wall clock across client construction, so they flake, and a backward clock step turns them into hard failures.**
`src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:1279‑1283`, `1332‑1336`, `1601‑1605`. `reset` is read from `SystemTime::now()` **before** `mount_flaky_server_error`, `MusicBrainzProvider::for_test` (which builds the reqwest client and may initialise the system trust store) and the first request; the code then recomputes `now` when the 503 lands (musicbrainz.rs:536‑543). The whole gap eats the 4 s slack the `>= 6s` assertion allows, and `cargo test` runs the suite in parallel on shared runners. Failure modes: (a) a gap >4 s makes `advanced >= 6` fail; (b) a gap >20 s pushes the hint past the 30 s cap, so the call errors on attempt 0 and `task.await.unwrap().unwrap()` panics. Symmetrically, `server_error_with_an_elapsed_reset_waits_the_backoff` computes `now - 60` up front (1499‑1503), so a backward clock step >60 s fails its `success_hits == 1`. Correct behaviour: the expected wait should not depend on when the *test* sampled the clock. Smallest fix: generate the header inside a `Respond` impl at respond time (`SystemTime::now().as_secs() + 10` per response), or add a `#[cfg(test)]`-overridable `epoch_now()` seam; that also makes the truncation/epoch math directly testable.

**2. MEDIUM — `is_format_character` does not cover the format characters its own doc names, and nothing tests it, so a hostile 5xx body can still smuggle invisible/ASCII-smuggling text into the operator log.**
`src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:639‑648` (doc 636‑638). Covered: 200B‑200F, 202A‑202E, 2060‑2064, 2066‑206F, FEFF. Missing Cf characters that are "invisible but reorder or hide the text around them" (the stated contract): **U+061C ARABIC LETTER MARK** (a bidi control with the same reordering power as the covered U+200F), U+00AD, U+180E, U+FFF9‑FFFB, U+110BD/U+110CD, U+13430‑1343F, U+1BCA0‑1BCA3, U+1D173‑1D17A, and **U+E0001 / U+E0020‑E007F (tag characters — the standard ASCII-smuggling vector)**. None of these is `is_control()` or `split_whitespace`, so they reach `tracing::warn!` intact. Separately, no test anywhere exercises `is_format_character` (grep: no `\u{200…}`/`\u{202…}`/`\u{FEFF}` in the module; `server_error_strips_control_characters_from_the_body` at 1636‑1671 only uses `\u{1b}`, `\u{0}`, `\u{7}`), so deleting `|| is_format_character(character)` leaves the suite green. Correct behaviour: strip the full Cf set that can hide/reorder text, and add one test that puts a bidi override (e.g. `\u{202E}`) and a tag character in the body/zone and asserts neither survives.

**3. MEDIUM — three decision paths added by this change are unguarded by tests: the reset-derived over-cap branch, the `<body omitted>` branch, and (unobservably) the byte-cap.**

1. **MEDIUM — non-UTF-8 (obs-text) header values vanish silently from the error detail.**

Smallest fix: add `'\u{061C}'` and `'\u{FFF9}'..='\u{FFFB}'` (optionally the tag range) to the `matches!` list.

## Review

**Read/checked:** `/tmp/review.diff` in full (1299 lines); `watchdog_diff --stat` to confirm the working tree matches (3 files, +1204/−14); full current contents of `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs` (all 2,790 lines, retry loop, helpers, constants, whole test module) and `src/discography/mod.rs` (`DiscographyError`, `from_error`, `is_stable_artist_resolution_failure`, `provider_error_reports_the_provider_kind`); README §"current MusicBrainz discovery limits"; all call sites of `DiscographyError` / `HttpStatus` / `from_error` in `src/`; `tests/` (no MusicBrainz coverage there). I could not run `cargo`; the supervisor should run `cargo test` (workspace root) and `cargo clippy --all-targets`.

**Correct (verified, not taken on trust)**
- `server_retry_hint` (`musicbrainz.rs:527-546`) really does max across repeated fields for both headers (`header_integer_max`, 551-562), filters zero/elapsed to `None`, and returns the later of the pair; `request_json:300-307` returns on `!within_cap` before any sleep and sleeps only ≤ 30 s, so no path sleeps > 2×30 s and no over-cap hint is ever slept on. `Duration::from_secs(u64::MAX)` reaches only the message, never `sleep`.
- `is_format_character` removal *is* caught: the test body at 2118 uses U+202E and U+E0041, neither of which is `char::is_control`, so `musicbrainz.rs:2143-2146` fails without the call.
- Cap boundary is pinned inclusively: `server_error_hint_at_the_cap_is_retried` (1630-1668) requires a 30 s sleep and the 31 s case (1441-1490) requires a single attempt.
- Body handling: single `read_limited` call per error; slice at 584 cannot panic on a split UTF-8 sequence (`from_utf8_lossy`); `<body omitted>`, truncation-before-normalisation, repeated headers, exhausted qualifier, unusable-value quoting all have tests.
- Classification: `from_error` catch-all still yields `Provider` (`mod.rs:687-692`); nothing in `src/` matches `HttpStatus(5xx)`; 429/4xx/transport branches are byte-for-byte unchanged (287-292, 309, 312-317).

**Findings (most serious first)**

1. **MEDIUM — `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:1671-1700` (`server_error_prefers_retry_after_when_it_is_later`): the reset is computed at mock-build time, so the test does not test the boundary it names and can be defeated by a `min`.** Lines 1677-1681 take `SystemTime::now()` *before* the mock is mounted and add 1; by the time the client evaluates it, `until_reset` is 0 or 1 s, which `Retry-After: 5` always dominates. The assertion `advanced ∈ [5, 7]` therefore passes for `a.max(b)`, for "Retry-After wins", and for `min` whenever the build→response gap crosses a second boundary (the reset then filters to `None` and the value is 5 again). It also contradicts round-3 fix #1 ("reset-based tests use an `OffsetResetResponder`"). Correct behaviour: the reset must be produced at respond time, e.g. `OffsetResetResponder { offset_secs: 2, additional_headers: vec![("retry-after", "5")], .. }`, which makes "5 s beats a 2 s reset" deterministic against both `min` and "reset wins".

2. **MEDIUM — `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:1987` (`server_error_reset_beyond_the_cap_is_not_retried`): `assert!(message.contains("120"))` is a wall-clock-second flake.** `OffsetResetResponder::respond` writes `now + 120`, but `provider_error` prints `wait.as_secs()` where `wait = epoch - SystemTime::now()` at the client (`musicbrainz.rs:531-537`, truncated with `as_secs`). Any second tick between the responder and the client makes the detail read "server asked to wait 119s" and the test fails although the code is correct — the same class of real-clock coupling round 3 removed from the other reset tests. Correct behaviour: assert the cap wording (`"not retried"`) and either drop the number or accept `119`/`120`; if the number must be exact, use a `Retry-After` (header value, not derived) as the other over-cap test does.

3. **LOW — `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:646-672` (`is_format_character`): the doc claims category Cf but five Cf code points are missing.** U+0600–U+0605 (Arabic number sign …), U+06DD, U+070F, U+0890–U+0891 and U+08E2 are Cf; U+0600–U+0605 are prepended concatenation marks that visually reorder following digits — exactly the "invisible but reorder or hide" property the doc cites. Either add those ranges or narrow the doc to "a curated subset of Cf" so the next reader doesn't assume completeness.

4. **LOW — `README.md:1135-1136` vs `musicbrainz.rs:266-267`: the cumulative-bound claim understates the real bound.** The README says "at most two such pauses (60 s) plus the per-attempt timeout" (read as 70 s), while every attempt carries its own `REQUEST_TIMEOUT` (`Client::builder().timeout(10 s)`, per request), so the worst case is 30 + 10 + 30 + 10 + 10 = **90 s** — which the code doc now states correctly as "two capped pauses plus three timeouts". The README should name both figures (or say "plus a 10 s timeout per attempt").

5. **LOW — `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:575-583`: the non-UTF-8 `Retry-After` path is untested although it is in the stated contract.** The only non-UTF-8 test (2137-2155) exercises `x-ratelimit-zone`. `ignored_retry_after` is the sole place that would surface a non-UTF-8 `Retry-After`; a regression to `to_str()` there would silently drop the value from the message and no test would fail. Add a 503 with `HeaderValue::from_bytes(b"5\x80")` and assert `"not honoured"`.

6. **LOW — `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:1620, 1799, 1851`: the three backoff tests cannot distinguish the 1 s first backoff from 2 s.** With `advanced >= 1` and `advanced <= 3`, a `backoff(attempt)` off-by-one (attempt 0 → 2 s) still lands at `advanced = 2` and passes, yet the assertion text says "must fall back to the one-second backoff". Tighten the upper bound to 2 s in these three tests.

7. **LOW — `src/discography/mod.rs:678-686` and `:3663`: the new variant's classification is only covered by the catch-all, and the doc enumeration is stale.** `from_error`'s doc lists "transport, HTTP status, decode, pagination, or unusable candidate data" but not `ProviderError`; the test named `provider_error_reports_the_provider_kind` feeds `DiscographyError::Transport` (`FakeProvider::failing`), not the new variant. Add `from_error(&ProviderError { status: 503, detail: .. }) == Provider` and `!is_stable_artist_resolution_failure(&ProviderError { .. })` so a future edit that moves the variant into the `Unresolved` arm is caught.

8. **LOW (verify, no code change) — `src/discography/musicbrainz.rs:511-526`: the `X-RateLimit-Reset` unit is an external assumption with a silent failure mode.** Nothing in the repo (no fixture, no captured response) pins the header to epoch seconds; if the provider ever sends delta-seconds, `epoch.saturating_sub(now)` collapses to 0, is filtered, and the code quietly retries 1 s later inside the closed window — the exact behaviour the change exists to prevent. Worth capturing one real 503 header set in the docs/test comments before relying on the reset half.

9. **LOW — Ctrl+C latency: `runner.rs:2619` / `:2856` check the cancellation flag only between artists/albums, and the new pauses are not raced against it.** A single request can now hold the process for ~90 s (was ~33 s: 10+1+10+2+10) before an interrupt is observed. Acceptable if the bound is intended; otherwise race the `sleep` against the flag.

10. **LOW (outside the diff) — `docs/agent/specs/2026-09-10-authoritative-artist-discography-design.md:225-226` and `:352-354` still document "HTTP 5xx responses retry after 1 second and then 2 seconds" and the old `Retry-After`-only limit.** The README was updated, the spec was not; update it if specs are treated as living contracts.

**Merge verdict: OK with notes.** No production defect found in the retry, cap, sanitisation or classification logic; the two MEDIUM items are test-strength/flake issues in newly added tests (fix 1 and 2 before treating the suite as guarding the "later of the two" rule), the rest are documentation and coverage notes.

All required reading is complete: the full diff, the full `musicbrainz.rs` (all 2,766 lines including the entire test module), the changed regions and surrounding code of `mod.rs` (error enum, `DiscoveryFailure::from_error`, failure-cache classification), plus bounded verification of the callers that consume these errors (runner warns, classify-all fallbacks in `mod.rs`; no other crate code matches on `DiscographyError::HttpStatus`/the new variant exhaustively), and `Cargo.toml` toolchain bounds (`rust-version = "1.88"`, `is_none_or` already used in `config.rs` — no API-compat issue).

## Review

**Round-3 fix verification (all six verified in current code, with tests that pin them):**
1. Respond-time reset (`OffsetResetResponder`, musicbrainz.rs:748-769) is used by `honors_rate_limit_reset`, `prefers_the_longer...`, `beyond_the_cap`, `elapsed_reset`, each with both lower and upper bounds — except one test, see Finding 2/3 below.
2. `is_format_character` (musicbrainz.rs:652-672) covers the complete current Cf set (checked range-by-range against Unicode Cf: 00AD, 061C, 180E, 200B–200F, 202A–202E, 2060–2064, 2066–206F, FFF9–FFFB, 110BD, 110CD, 13430–1343F, 1BCA0–1BCA3, 1D173–1D17A, E0001, E0020–E007F, FEFF — nothing missing); `server_error_strips_format_characters_from_the_body` (2101-2135) strips U+202E and U+E0041, which are neither control chars nor whitespace, so it fails if `is_format_character` were dropped from `single_line`. (Zl/Zp line separators aren't Cf but are White_Space, so `split_whitespace` collapses them — no log-injection residue.)
3. Over-cap reset, `<body omitted>`, truncation-before-normalisation (the only printable word sits past the 4096-byte cut, so the assert fails if the order flipped), repeated headers (passes `advanced >= 2`, which fails if the first value `0` won), non-UTF-8 header — all present and decisive.
4. `header_integer_max` (551-559) takes max across all fields for both `retry-after` and `x-ratelimit-reset`; the repeated-field boundary is test-pinned for `retry-after`.
5. Lossy decode for zone (566-569) and unusable Retry-After (571-578), pinned by the non-UTF-8 zone test.
6. Docs match behaviour: enum doc's empty-detail rule (mod.rs:113-123) matches the code exactly (all whitespace/empty-sanitising cases are pre-filtered); the header-unit claim and the exhausted-hint/retries-exhausted wording match.

**Behavior walks verified (evidence, not summary):** all five `intent` bullets traced line-by-line through `request_json` (280-310), `server_retry_hint` (527-549, including the pre-epoch-clock `map_or(epoch, …)` clamp — it computes wait 0 and falls back to `saturating_sub`-safe backoff, never an unbounded sleep), `provider_error`, `backoff`, `parse_retry_after`; 429/transport/success/pagination paths byte-identical to pre-diff structure; per-call sleeps hard-capped at two (attempt 0 and 1 only; attempt 2 returns before sleeping); single body read per error (body is only touched on the return path); exhausted retry fairness (paths never attempt twice past exhaustion); no compile break introduced by the variant (only catch-all matches exist).

### Findings (all LOW — nothing rose to MEDIUM/HIGH)

**Finding 1: LOW — README understates the per-request worst-case wait vs the code's own doc.**
- Where: README.md:1135-1136 ("One request spends at most two such pauses (60 s) plus the per-attempt timeout").
- What: there are three attempts, each carrying a 10 s timeout, so the worst hold is ≈ 60 s of sleeps + 30 s of timeouts (+ ~2 s pacing) ≈ 92 s. The singular "the per-attempt timeout" reads as one 10 s addend (70 s), while `request_json`'s doc (musicbrainz.rs:266-267) correctly says "three timeouts", and the two docs therefore disagree; as a strict maximum the README sentence is false.
- Fix: "plus three per-attempt timeouts" (or "at most two pauses plus the per-attempt timeouts, i.e. at most ~92 s"). Smallest edit: add "s" — one word.

## Review

### Correct (verified, not merely trusted)

- **5xx hint selection** (`musicbrainz.rs:293-308`, `527-543`): the branch sleeps `max(Retry-After delta, reset − now)` and uses `backoff(attempt)` only via `hint.unwrap_or_else`, so the local backoff is unreachable whenever either field is usable.
